question: An AA battery is much bigger than an AAA, yet one key number printed on both is exactly the same. What is it?
source_excerpt: Sources agree on a 1.5 V nominal rating for alkaline AA batteries.

extra.why_interesting: Most people assume a bigger battery is a 'stronger' battery. The surprise is that the fat AA and the skinny AAA push electricity equally hard. The AA just keeps going for longer.
extra.verification_notes: AA and AAA alkaline cells are both nominally 1.5 V (NiMH are 1.2 V on both sizes), so the shared number holds; the search returned only low-quality pages and no AAA-specific figures, so the AAA half rests on general knowledge, and no newer developments change it.

explanation: Voltage comes from the chemistry inside, not from the size. A bigger battery simply holds more of the same chemicals, so it lasts longer rather than pushing harder.

question: On a freezing night your torch dies, but after a few minutes in your warm pocket the same batteries work again. Why?
alternative_answers: chemical reactions slow in the cold
the chemistry works better when warm
source_excerpt: The Arrhenius equation governs reaction rates, showing that chemical reactions slow exponentially as temperature decreases.

extra.why_interesting: People assume a battery that dies in the cold is used up. In fact its energy is all still there. The chemical reaction has just slowed down, and warmth brings the battery back, which feels almost like magic.
extra.verification_notes: Cold slows the battery's electrochemical reactions and raises internal resistance, a reversible effect that warming undoes (https://www.batterytender.com/blogs/battery-tender-blog/why-car-batteries-die-in-cold-weather-the-complete-scientific-explanation).

explanation: A battery makes electricity through a chemical reaction, and cold makes that reaction sluggish, so the battery can't deliver enough current. Warm it up and the reaction speeds up again, because the energy was there all along.
